summary:
Second Samuel, the second half of the single Hebrew book of Samuel, covers the reign of David, commonly dated around 1010–970 BC — his rise, and then its long unraveling. It opens with David's lament over Saul and Jonathan, built on the refrain "How the mighty have fallen!" (1:19, 25, 27). Anointed king at Hebron by his own tribe of Judah (anointing — oil poured on the head — marked God's chosen), David outlasts Saul's surviving house in a drawn-out war and is then anointed by all Israel: king at thirty, reigning forty years (5:4). He captures the fortress of Zion — Jerusalem, a city the Jebusites had held against Israel since the conquest (Joshua 15:63) — and makes it his capital, the City of David. The ark of the covenant, the chest that marked God's presence, comes up to the city with David dancing "with all his might" (6:14), while Saul's daughter Michal despises him for it.

Settled in a cedar palace, David proposes to build God a house — a temple in place of the ark's tent. Through Nathan the prophet, God reverses the offer: David will not build God a house; God will build David one — a dynasty. "Your house and kingdom will endure forever before Me, and your throne will be established forever" (7:16). The promise, often called the Davidic covenant, stands behind the prophets' hope of a coming king from David's line; the New Testament opens by calling Jesus "the son of David" (Matthew 1:1), and Gabriel restates it to Mary — the throne of "His father David" and a kingdom that "will never end" (Luke 1:32–33).

Chapter 11 is the turn. "In the spring, at the time when kings march out to war... David remained in Jerusalem" (11:1). He takes Bathsheba, wife of Uriah the Hittite, one of his elite soldiers; when she conceives and Uriah cannot be induced to go home to her, David has him left to die at the fiercest point of a siege. The narrator adds a single verdict: "the thing that David had done was evil in the sight of the LORD" (11:27). Nathan returns with a parable of a rich man who steals a poor man's one ewe lamb, waits for David's outrage, then says, "You are that man!" (12:7). David repents — the heading of Psalm 51 places that psalm here — but the sentence stands: "the sword will never depart from your house" (12:10). The child dies. Amnon, David's firstborn, rapes his half-sister Tamar; her brother Absalom murders Amnon and later mounts a revolt that sends David up the Mount of Olives weeping and barefoot (15:30). When Joab, David's general, kills Absalom against explicit orders, the king's grief swallows the victory: "O my son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you" (18:33).

The final chapters are appendices: a famine, Philistine exploits, David's song of deliverance (chapter 22, repeated with small differences as Psalm 18), his last words, and the roll of his mighty men — a list that ends with Uriah the Hittite (23:39). Last comes the census: "the anger of the LORD" stirs David to count Israel's fighting men (24:1); the retelling in 1 Chronicles 21:1 names Satan as the inciter, a difference readers have long noted. A plague kills seventy thousand and halts at the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite, which David buys — "I will not offer to the LORD my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing" (24:24) — to build an altar. According to 2 Chronicles 3:1, that threshing floor on Mount Moriah became the site of Solomon's temple.
